_comment: English texts of the ideas map (site/karta-idey.en.src.html): the same ids as lessons/shared/ideas-map.json; years, lanes, lessons, paper links and parent links are taken from the Russian file at build time (site/build.py), only title, org, problem and contribution (shown as “Solution”) (and short, the chip label of a long title) are translated here. The texts follow the same plain-language rules and limits: problem ≤ 130 characters, contribution ≤ 260. Model names stay as in the papers.

nodes.title: Dijkstra
nodes.problem: There are far too many paths on a map to try them all and pick the shortest one.
nodes.contribution: The algorithm spreads out from the start like a wave and remembers the shortest path to every cell, so the first path to reach the goal is the shortest. Many robots still plan their paths this way today.

nodes.title: Kalman filter
nodes.problem: No sensor knows exactly where the robot is: each one is wrong in its own way.
nodes.contribution: At every step the filter first predicts where the robot will be, then corrects the prediction with a sensor reading and decides by itself which one to trust more. Several imprecise sources add up to one precise estimate.

nodes.title: A*
nodes.problem: Dijkstra’s algorithm searches in all directions at once, even away from the goal, and wastes time on it.
nodes.contribution: A* first checks the cells through which the path to the goal comes out shorter, counting the rest of the way in a straight line, ignoring walls. It finds the same shortest path but checks far fewer cells. It was made for the Shakey robot.

nodes.title: PD controller
nodes.problem: A policy sets a joint angle, but a motor can only turn, so the arm overshoots the target or sags under its weight.
nodes.contribution: The controller pulls the joint to the target angle like a spring and damps its speed like a shock absorber. Takegaki and Arimoto proved that, with the arm’s weight compensated, it always reaches the target. Almost every walking policy relies on it today.

nodes.title: Impedance control
nodes.problem: If the camera is off and the target ends up under the table, an arm that insists on the target presses harder and harder.
nodes.contribution: Hogan proposed specifying how the arm responds to obstacles: the controller makes it act like a spring of chosen stiffness. Then a camera error makes the arm press on the table only gently.

nodes.title: ALVINN
nodes.problem: No one can write driving rules for every road.
nodes.contribution: A neural network learned to drive a van by watching a person drive it. It was the first robot trained from demonstrations.

nodes.title: Series elastic actuator (SEA)
nodes.problem: A geared motor is strong but stiff: its output force is hard to set precisely, and impacts hit the gears directly.
nodes.contribution: Pratt and Williamson placed a spring between the motor and what it moves. Its compression tells the robot the exact force to control, and on impact the spring gives first. Such actuators drive the legs of the ANYmal walking robot.

nodes.title: RRT
nodes.problem: An arm with seven joints has so many possible positions that a grid search like A* cannot cope.
nodes.contribution: RRT grows a tree of paths from the start: it picks a random point and extends a branch toward it from the nearest part of the tree if nothing is in the way. If a path to the goal exists, the tree finds it sooner or later, with no grid needed.

nodes.title: Particle filter
nodes.problem: A Kalman filter keeps one guess of where the robot is, and in a house with two identical bedrooms it can be confidently wrong.
nodes.contribution: A particle filter tracks many guesses at once, scattered over the map as dots, and keeps those that best match the sensors. The robot holds both bedrooms in mind until it can tell them apart and can find itself on the map from scratch.

nodes.title: DAgger
nodes.problem: A policy trained from demonstrations sooner or later ends up where the expert never went and does not know what to do.
nodes.contribution: The policy drives on its own, and an expert labels the right action wherever it ends up. The labels are added to the data and the policy is trained again, so it learns to recover from its own mistakes.

nodes.title: RRT*
nodes.problem: RRT finds a path, but usually a crooked and long one, and it does not get shorter however long the tree grows.
nodes.contribution: RRT* attaches each new branch to the tree in the shortest way and reconnects neighbouring branches if the new one gives them a shorter route. The longer the tree grows, the closer the path gets to the shortest one.

nodes.title: Transformer
nodes.problem: Neural networks read text one word after another, trained slowly and struggled to connect words far apart.
nodes.contribution: A transformer works with a sequence of pieces, such as words, parts of an image or actions, and each piece chooses by itself which others to look at. The same design fits text, images and actions, and RT-1, ACT and π0 are built on it.

nodes.title: PPO
nodes.problem: If a policy changes a lot in one training step, it breaks, and if it changes little, it learns too slowly.
nodes.contribution: PPO limits how much the policy can change in one update. The simple and stable method became the standard way to train robots in simulation.

nodes.title: SAC
nodes.problem: PPO learns only from fresh experience and throws it away after each update, while every trial on a real robot is costly.
nodes.contribution: SAC stores its experience and learns from it many times, and it gets a reward bonus for varied actions, so it keeps trying new things. Later, with SAC, a four-legged robot learned to walk in a couple of hours in the real world.

nodes.title: World Models
nodes.problem: Trying actions in the real world is slow and costly, and a policy that sees only images learns slowly.
nodes.contribution: The world model compresses a game frame into a few numbers and predicts what the game will show next, and a small controller learns to act on these numbers. In VizDoom it was trained entirely in the model’s imagination and worked in the real game.

nodes.title: DeepMimic
nodes.problem: No one knows how to write the reward “walk like a human” as a formula, so gaits come out unnatural.
nodes.contribution: The policy is rewarded for how closely it follows a recording of human motion. With one short recording per skill, a simulated character learned to walk, run and do flips.

nodes.title: Dactyl
nodes.problem: A five-fingered hand needs a huge number of attempts, and there is no way to collect them on a real hand.
nodes.contribution: The policy was trained in a simulator that slightly changed the physics and the look of the scene every time, gathering about a hundred years of experience. On a real hand it turns a cube without a single real attempt in training.

nodes.title: MPC Cheetah 3
nodes.problem: A controller looks only at the current error and pulls straight toward the target, even into a dead end.
nodes.contribution: Model predictive control (MPC) uses a model of the robot to pick the best plan for the near future, executes only its start and plans again. In Cheetah 3 a plan takes under a millisecond, and the four-legged robot trots and even gallops.

nodes.title: RoboNet
nodes.problem: Each lab collects data on its own robot, and a model trained on that data works only there.
nodes.contribution: Different robots in several labs recorded their random movements into one open dataset. After training on it, a new robot needs only a few hundred recordings of its own.

nodes.title: Dreamer
nodes.problem: Learning inside a world model’s imagination looked only a few steps ahead and failed on long tasks.
nodes.contribution: Dreamer trains the policy entirely on imagined trials inside the world model and learns to estimate how much reward lies further ahead. Later versions master Atari games, control tasks and Minecraft with one algorithm.

nodes.title: Transporter
nodes.problem: A policy that outputs coordinates as numbers needs many demonstrations, and a shifted object is a new task for it.
nodes.contribution: Transporter marks on a top view of the table where to pick an object and finds where to place it by matching the image patch around the object against the whole scene. Shifts do not confuse it, and sometimes one demonstration is enough.

nodes.title: ViT
nodes.problem: A transformer reads a sequence of words, while an image is a grid of pixels.
nodes.contribution: The image is cut into small squares that are fed to a transformer in order, like words. Trained on hundreds of millions of images, it recognizes pictures better than earlier vision networks.

nodes.title: Teacher and student
nodes.problem: A policy trained on random worlds in a simulator does not know which world it got, so it prepares for the worst.
nodes.contribution: A teacher first learns to walk knowing everything about the world: friction, terrain, foot contacts. A student then learns to copy it from the robot’s sensors and their recent history. ANYmal crossed mud, snow and streams after training only on hard ground.

nodes.title: CLIP
nodes.problem: A vision network knew only a fixed list of objects, and there was no way to name a new object to it in words.
nodes.contribution: The model was trained on hundreds of millions of internet images to tell which caption fits which image. Any object can now be found by words, and CLIPort, PerAct and many vision-language models rely on CLIP.

nodes.title: CLIPort
nodes.problem: Transporter can pick and place but does not understand which object to move or where to put it.
nodes.contribution: CLIPort joins two networks: CLIP understands from words what to pick, and Transporter finds where it is and where to place it. The robot follows commands in words and often handles colours and objects that were not in the demonstrations.

nodes.title: Walking in minutes
nodes.problem: Walking takes a huge number of steps in simulation, and an ordinary simulator needs hours to produce them.
nodes.contribution: The simulator and the training run on one graphics card, where a whole crowd of robots walks at the same time. A policy for walking on flat ground is ready in four minutes, and many legged robots, humanoids included, now learn to walk this way.

nodes.title: BC-Z
nodes.problem: A policy trained from demonstrations can do one task and does not understand commands in words.
nodes.contribution: One neural network was trained on demonstrations of a hundred tasks and is given the command in words. The robot carried out some new commands without a single example, and later such policies performed the steps of SayCan plans.

nodes.title: SayCan
nodes.problem: A language model knows the steps of “make coffee” but knows neither the robot nor its kitchen.
nodes.contribution: The next step is chosen by two scores: the language model says how useful it is for the task, and the robot estimates whether it can succeed right now. This turns ready-made skills into plans the robot can carry out.

nodes.title: Inner Monologue
nodes.problem: When a step fails, the language model in SayCan never learns about it and goes on as if everything were done.
nodes.contribution: After each step the robot tells the model in words what happened: whether the step worked, what is on the table, what a person answered. The model repeats a failed step or changes the plan by itself, without any retraining.

nodes.title: Code as Policies
nodes.problem: A planner like SayCan picks only from ready-made skills, and “move the cup a bit to the left” is not on such a list.
nodes.contribution: A language model writes a program for the robot: it calls the robot’s vision and motion functions, computes coordinates and writes the missing functions itself. This lets the robot follow commands with numbers and conditions.

nodes.title: PerAct
nodes.problem: A top view of the table is enough to pick and place, but opening a drawer needs the position of the arm in space.
nodes.contribution: PerAct divides the space above the table into cubes and chooses in which cube and with what rotation to put the gripper next. An ordinary planner moves the arm between these points, and one model performs many tasks from commands in words.

nodes.title: RT-1
nodes.problem: Before, a separate model was trained for each robot task.
nodes.contribution: One model performs more than 700 different kitchen tasks from camera frames and a command in words. It outputs actions as tokens, the way a language model outputs words.

nodes.title: JEPA
nodes.problem: Models that learn without labels by guessing the pixels of a hidden part of an image waste effort on noise and small details.
nodes.contribution: Instead of the pixels of the hidden part, JEPA guesses its short description, which the model has learned itself. The model captures what is in the image without wasting effort on trifles. The same scheme was later applied to video.

nodes.title: Diffusion Policy
nodes.problem: If a task can be done in several ways, an ordinary policy averages them and does something in between that is wrong.
nodes.contribution: The policy builds several next actions at once from random noise, cleaning it up step by step, like image generators. It picks one way and sticks to it.

nodes.title: ACT
nodes.problem: Precise two-armed robots are expensive, and cheap arms are too imprecise for fine work like inserting a battery.
nodes.contribution: ACT outputs a whole action chunk in one pass of the network and updates it 50 times a second, smoothing the joins between chunks. This let the low-cost two-armed robot ALOHA learn fine work from a small number of demonstrations.

nodes.title: KnowNo
nodes.problem: With two bowls on the table, “put the bowl in the microwave” is ambiguous, but a language model confidently picks one.
nodes.contribution: The model proposes options, and KnowNo uses examples checked in advance to keep only those that can be trusted. If more than one remains, the robot asks a person and completes tasks with a reliability set beforehand.

nodes.title: RT-2
nodes.problem: A robot knows only the objects it has seen in its demonstrations.
nodes.contribution: A model that already understands images and text from the internet was fine-tuned on robot actions. The robot began to follow commands about things that were not in its data, such as “move the can to Taylor Swift”.

nodes.title: VoxPoser
nodes.problem: Ready-made pick-and-place skills cannot be combined into a motion that brings the arm to a drawer handle and avoids a vase.
nodes.contribution: A language model writes code that marks up the space above the table: where the arm should reach and what to keep away from. An ordinary planner builds a path on this map, and nothing has to be trained for the task.

nodes.title: BridgeData V2
nodes.problem: RoboNet’s random movements teach no skills, and demonstrations of one task in one room do not carry over to others.
nodes.contribution: Tens of thousands of demonstrations of different skills were recorded on a low-cost WidowX arm in many settings, with tasks labelled in words. Octo, OpenVLA and other models are tested on this dataset.

nodes.title: MimicGen
nodes.problem: Demonstrations are recorded by a person, and every new arrangement of objects means recording them again.
nodes.contribution: MimicGen cuts a demonstration into pieces by subtask and fits each piece to the new object positions, and the simulator keeps only successful attempts. A few human recordings turn into tens of thousands of new ones.

nodes.title: Open X-Embodiment
nodes.problem: Each lab has its own robot and few recordings, while large models were trained on one company’s robots.
nodes.contribution: Labs around the world pooled their recordings into one open dataset with over a million episodes from very different robots. Models trained on this mix work better than those trained on one robot’s data.

nodes.title: Mobile ALOHA
nodes.problem: The two-armed ALOHA stands at a table, but housework means driving around the kitchen, opening cabinets and calling a lift.
nodes.contribution: The ALOHA arms were put on a wheeled base that the operator pushes while strapped to it with a belt. Once old tabletop demonstrations were added to the new ones, the robot called the lift almost every time, and without them it never did.

nodes.title: OK-Robot
nodes.problem: “Pick up A and put it in B” has to work in an unfamiliar home, without collecting data there or retraining anything.
nodes.contribution: OK-Robot is assembled from ready-made open models and classical algorithms: neural networks find objects and how to grasp them, and A* plans the route. Without any retraining, the robot completed more than half of the tasks in homes it had never seen.

nodes.title: Genie and Cosmos
nodes.problem: Dreamer learns inside one game, but a model is needed that learns from internet video how any scene changes after an action.
nodes.contribution: Genie learned from game videos by itself what actions exist and creates a controllable world from a single picture. NVIDIA’s Cosmos video models are open and are fine-tuned for robots to generate data and test policies.

nodes.title: UMI
nodes.problem: A robot cannot be carried around other people’s homes, so demonstrations are recorded in a few labs, in the same scenes.
nodes.contribution: UMI replaces the robot with a handheld gripper with a camera, so demonstrations can be recorded anywhere. A policy trained on recordings from many places usually succeeded in new places, while one trained in a single lab never did.

nodes.title: DROID
nodes.problem: Bridge was recorded at one institute in toy kitchens, so its scenes are not varied enough for new places.
nodes.contribution: The same setup, an arm on a cart, was built at many institutes and recorded demonstrations in hundreds of different rooms. With this data, policies work more reliably in new places.

nodes.title: H2O
nodes.problem: A humanoid has to copy a person’s whole-body motion in real time, but many human recordings are beyond its abilities.
nodes.contribution: Human motion recordings were first checked in a simulator, keeping those the robot can repeat. The policy trained on them works on the real humanoid right away and copies the motion of a person seen by an ordinary camera.

nodes.title: Octo
nodes.problem: The best model on Open X-Embodiment data is closed, and an arm with other cameras and joints cannot be connected to it.
nodes.contribution: Octo was made open and small, and a new camera or a new way of control is added without rebuilding the model. It is fine-tuned for a new robot in a few hours on one graphics card.

nodes.title: HumanPlus
nodes.problem: Tasks with soft objects cannot be learned in a simulator, and controlling a real humanoid’s whole body is costly and hard.
nodes.contribution: The humanoid copies the motion of an operator filmed by an ordinary webcam, using a policy trained in a simulator. From a few dozen such demonstrations the robot learned to put on a shoe, stand up and walk by itself.

nodes.title: OpenVLA
nodes.problem: Models like RT-2, built on a vision-language model, were closed, so no one could fine-tune them in their own lab.
nodes.contribution: OpenVLA was built on an open language model and, like RT-2, taught to output actions. It completes more tasks than the closed RT-2-X and can be fine-tuned in any lab on one graphics card.

nodes.title: PaliGemma
nodes.problem: Models that control robots need a small open model that understands images and text.
nodes.contribution: Google released a small open model that answers questions about images and adapts well to new tasks through fine-tuning. π0 and π0.5 are built on it.

nodes.title: HIL-SERL
nodes.problem: A policy trained from demonstrations is never better than its operator, and learning by trial on a real robot seemed too slow.
nodes.contribution: The robot learns from reward in the real world, starting from demonstrations, and a person takes over when it makes mistakes. In a couple of hours the policy succeeds almost every time and works faster than one trained on the same demonstrations.

nodes.title: π0
nodes.problem: Models that output actions as words are too slow for smooth movements.
nodes.contribution: A small separate network was added to a vision-language model to output a smooth chunk of movements quickly. One model folds laundry, clears tables and assembles boxes.

nodes.title: Helix
nodes.problem: A humanoid’s arms and fingers need commands 200 times a second, and a large vision-language model is far slower.
nodes.contribution: A slow, large model decides what to do a few times a second, and a fast, small network follows its hint to move the arms, fingers and torso. Both run on the robot itself.

nodes.title: AgiBot World
nodes.problem: DROID robots have one arm and no one checks the recordings by hand, while models need a bigger and cleaner dataset.
nodes.contribution: A fleet of identical two-armed robots recorded over a million demonstrations, and people checked every one. A model trained on this dataset does noticeably better at tasks than after training on Open X-Embodiment.

nodes.title: GR00T N1
nodes.problem: Only what Figure chose to tell is known about Helix, and there was no open model of this kind for humanoids.
nodes.contribution: NVIDIA released an open model with a slow part that understands the scene and the command and a fast part that outputs a chunk of movements. It was trained on robot recordings, simulator data and videos of people.

nodes.title: Gemini Robotics
nodes.problem: A large model that reasons about the world does not fit on a robot and answers in seconds, but the robot needs to act faster.
nodes.contribution: The main part of the Gemini-based model runs in the cloud, and a part on board the robot turns its answer into a chunk of movements. About a quarter of a second passes from a camera frame to movement.

nodes.title: π0.5
nodes.problem: π0 worked well where it had been fine-tuned, but another home has different dishes, furniture and light.
nodes.contribution: The model was trained on a mix of very different data: recordings from homes, other robots, subtasks in words and images from the internet. It says by itself what to do next and cleans kitchens and bedrooms in homes it has never seen.

nodes.title: TWIST
nodes.problem: To collect data for whole-body tasks, the operator has to control every joint of the humanoid, legs included.
nodes.contribution: Motion capture cameras film the operator, and a policy repeats the operator’s pose in every joint of the robot, legs included. The robot lagged almost a second behind the person, and the next version, TWIST2, cut the delay.

nodes.title: V-JEPA 2
nodes.problem: A world model for a robot should learn from the robot’s recordings, but these are few compared to internet video.
nodes.contribution: The model learns to understand video from a million hours of internet clips, then learns to predict the results of actions from a small set of robot recordings. With its predictions, an arm moves objects in an unfamiliar lab.

nodes.title: π0.7
nodes.problem: Trained on a mix of recordings, the model works like an average operator, and there was no way to ask it to act like the best.
nodes.contribution: Along with the command, the model gets hints: which subtask to do, a picture of the goal, the desired speed and quality. It combines familiar skills into new tasks and folds laundry on a robot for which there were no laundry recordings.

nodes.title: End-to-end visuomotor policy
nodes.problem: Separate modules for seeing, planning and control each add errors at the seams, and a precise task fails.
nodes.contribution: A single neural network turns the camera image straight into motor commands and is trained as a whole, from pixels to actions. The robot fitted a block into a toy shape sorter almost every time, while a system of separate modules never did.

nodes.title: DayDreamer
nodes.problem: A simulator does not capture all the complexity of the real world, and model-free methods run out of hours on a real robot.
nodes.contribution: Dreamer was run unchanged on real robots: the A1 quadruped learned to roll over, stand up and walk in about an hour, and arms learned to move objects in a few hours.
